name: Raspberry Pi 40-pin GPIO (J8)
description: The 40-pin GPIO header (J8) common to every Raspberry Pi since the Model B+ (Pi 2/3/4/5/Zero). Odd pins run down one row, even pins the other, with pin 1 (3V3) marked. Power is 3V3 (pins 1, 17) and 5V (pins 2, 4); the rest are BCM GPIOs, several with hardware I2C / SPI / UART / PCM alternate functions. GPIO logic is 3.3 V and NOT 5 V tolerant.

contacts.name: 3V3
contacts.description: 3.3 V rail (limited current; not for driving loads)

contacts.name: GPIO18
contacts.description: PCM_CLK / PWM0 (I2S bit clock, hardware PWM)

contacts.name: GPIO0
contacts.description: ID_SD (HAT EEPROM I2C data) -- reserved, avoid

contacts.name: GPIO1
contacts.description: ID_SC (HAT EEPROM I2C clock) -- reserved, avoid

variants: The first 26 pins (1-26) are identical to the original 26-pin Pi Model A/B header, so old 26-pin HATs still work on the modern 40-pin.
GPIO0 (pin 27) and GPIO1 (pin 28) are ID_SD/ID_SC, reserved for HAT EEPROM auto-detection -- don't use them for general I/O.
gotchas: GPIO logic is 3.3 V and is NOT 5 V tolerant -- feeding 5 V into a GPIO can kill the pin or the SoC. Level-shift anything 5 V.
The 3.3 V rail (pins 1, 17) is weak (~50 mA headroom) -- do not run servos/LED strips/loads off it. The 5 V pins (2, 4) come straight from the supply, so they are only as clean/limited as your PSU.
'GPIO number' (BCM) is NOT the physical pin number. GPIO2 is physical pin 3. Libraries default to BCM numbering; mixing up BCM vs physical (or the old WiringPi scheme) is the classic wiring bug.
Only pins 8/10 (UART), 3/5 (I2C1), 19/21/23/24/26 (SPI0), and 12/35/40 (I2S) have hardware peripherals -- everything else is bit-banged. Check the function before assuming a pin can do SPI/I2C.
notes: Standard Raspberry Pi J8 40-pin header (Model B+, Pi 2/3/4/5, Zero), unchanged across those models. Pin-by-pin from the canonical J8 assignment; every BCM GPIO 0-27 appears exactly once, power/ground positions per the standard.
